To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) employee entitlements are a major issue of public policy concern, (ii) employees are involuntary lenders of their capital to their employer, (iii) employees have limited information, monitoring or voice rights within their employing organisations, (iv) these rights should be extended to reduce risk to employee entitlements and to ensure that employers have access to this capital, (v) this can be achieved through the introduction of employee ownership and (vi) this can be done without any loss of employee control

employee capital is a significant component of the capital structure of many Australian firms, employee capital is under-represented in the governance of firms, employee capital can be protected by the introduction of employee voice rights in the form of employee representation on the board of directors.

the Australian corporate governance system has not been effective in protecting the interests of employees and that the current system does not provide sufficient information, monitoring or voice rights to employees in the event that an employer becomes insolvent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the protection of employee capital in the form of employee entitlements and the rights that employees should have to monitor and influence the use of their capital in the workplace.

the following issues: 1) the extent to which employees are involuntary lenders of financial capital to their employers; 2) the extent to, and manner in which, employees are denied information, monitoring, and voice within their organisations; and 3) the extent to and manner in which employee entitlements can be protected through the provision of information, monitoring and employee voice rights.
employee capital and the protection of employee entitlement rights in the context of corporate governance and industrial democracy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Australian industrial relations system has failed to protect employee entitlements.
employee entitlements should not be protected by government regulation but rather by the granting of employee capital rights to the employer.

there are a number of reasons why employees should have the right to be informed about the financial state of their employer, the right to monitor the use of their capital and the right to voice their views on the management of their employer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are arguing that employee rights should be extended in order to protect employee entitlements.
employee rights to information, monitoring and participation in the workplace can be seen as an alternative to the protection of entitlements through the law.

the employee voice and monitoring role is important in protecting employee entitlements, and that employee voice is a necessary but not sufficient condition for the protection of employee entitlement rights.
The main takeaway from our work is that
employee entitlements are an issue for both corporate governance and industrial democracy.
employee entitlements can be protected by granting employees the same information, monitoring and decision rights as shareholders and other creditors of a company.
there is a need for a more balanced approach to employee entitlements.
